notes.meaning: Job contrasts his past honor with his present humiliation. In his culture, young people were expected to respect their elders, but now even young men laugh at him. Their fathers were so unreliable and worthless that Job would not have trusted them even to help his sheep dogs guard the flocks.

Job explains that these men and their fathers were completely useless for honest work. They lacked strength and vigor, having wasted away through laziness and poor living. They had nothing helpful to offer when young, and they reached old age without wisdom or honor.

These outcasts lived in extreme hunger and poverty, wandering through barren wastelands. Because of their shameful behavior, they stayed far away from civilized towns and hid in desolate deserts. They survived only by gnawing on whatever dry shrubs they could find on the scorched ground.

To stay alive, these desperate people picked salty leaves from wild bushes and dug up the bitter roots of broom plants. People only ate such foul-tasting roots when they were starving. Their miserable diet showed just how low they had sunk.

Townspeople drove these vagrants away from society whenever they showed up. People shouted warnings after them as if chasing away common thieves. Because they refused to work honestly, everyone treated them as dangerous nuisances.

Banished from human communities, they were forced to dwell in dark, gloomy valleys. They sheltered in rocky crevices and dirt holes in the ground like wild animals. Living in such rough caves was considered a sign of extreme misery.

Driven by hunger and distress, they cried out among the desert bushes like wild donkeys braying for food. They huddled together under prickly nettles and brambles to find shelter from the weather or to hide from the law.

These mockers were the children of foolish, godless parents who had no good name or reputation. They were regarded as the lowest scum of the earth and were beaten out of the settled land. Job highlights their shameful origin to show how deep his own humiliation is, since even they now look down on him.

Job has now become the subject of their mocking songs and campfire jokes. His name is used as a proverb of ruin and disgrace among the lowest class of people. In this unfair mockery, commentators see a clear picture of Jesus Christ, who was also ridiculed by sinners.

These outcasts despise Job and keep away from his loathsome disease, yet they draw near enough to show open contempt by spitting at him. In the ancient Near East, spitting in someone's presence was the ultimate insult. This cruel treatment also reminds believers of the shame Jesus bore when soldiers spat upon Him.

Job explains why these men dare to treat him so poorly: God has stripped away his strength and unstrung his defense, leaving him helpless. Seeing that God has afflicted Job and removed his former authority, his tormentors cast off all restraint and behave boldly against him.

A crowd of low-born youths rises up on Job's right hand, which was the traditional position of an accuser in a courtroom. They shove him, trip his feet, and attack him as if they were building dirt ramps to besiege a fortress. They use every effort to push an already broken man toward destruction.

The attackers ruin Job's paths so that he has no way of escape, and they block any relief from reaching him. They take spiteful pleasure in speeding up his ruin, even though they gain nothing from his misery. They do all this cruel mischief on their own without needing anyone to spur them on.
Job pictures his enemies storming in like an army through a wide breach in a battered city wall. They pour in like an irresistible flood or falling rubble, rolling over him in the midst of his ruins.

Overwhelming terrors now pursue Job from every direction like a violent windstorm. His noble reputation and personal dignity have been blown away, and his past prosperity has vanished as quickly as a morning cloud.

Job describes the total collapse of his inner spirit, saying his soul is poured out like spilled water in endless weeping. He feels as though days of relentless suffering have seized him, like an officer arresting a helpless debtor.
Night brings no rest or relief to Job, only sharper pain that feels like a sword piercing deep into his bones. His intense, gnawing aches continue around the clock, refusing to let him sleep.

Job's painful disease has completely disfigured his clothing. Fluid running from his sores has made his garments stiff and filthy, causing them to cling tightly to him like a tight neck collar. He feels as though his illness has grabbed him by the throat like an armed attacker.

Job feels that God has thrown him down into the mire and treated him like filth. His dark, scabbed skin and wasted body look like nothing more than a pile of dirt and ashes. He sees himself brought down to the very lowest state of human misery.

Job turns directly to God with urgent cries for help, but heaven seems completely silent. Even when he stands up and perseveres in prayer, God only seems to watch his agony coldly without stepping in to rescue him. Feeling ignored by God is the bitterest part of his entire trial.

In his intense anguish, Job speaks rashly and accuses God of becoming cruel and unmerciful toward him. He feels that the Almighty is using all His immense strength to oppose and crush him as if He were an enemy. Commentators point out that harboring such bitter thoughts of God was Job's great weakness during this trial.

Job feels as fragile and helpless as dry straw swept up by a violent storm wind. God has lifted him up into the tempest only to toss him about in terror, melting away his bodily strength and all his former substance.
Job is convinced that his illness will end in his physical death. He refers to the grave as a house appointed by God for all living creatures, where both rich and poor must eventually rest together.

Job comforts himself with the thought that his trials will finally end at the grave. God will not continue striking or afflicting a man once he is resting in the dust. Even though people cry out in distress while dying, death itself will provide a quiet shelter from earthly misery.

Job's conscience reminds him that in his prosperous days, he always wept for the afflicted and cared tenderly for the poor. He knows he was not hard-hearted or cruel toward others when they were in trouble. Remembering his past kindness brings him some comfort during his own crisis.

Because Job had loved God and shown mercy to others, he expected his life to continue in peace and prosperity. Instead, shocking disaster overtook him, and deep darkness fell where he looked for light. This terrible letdown made his suffering far harder to bear.

Job describes his deep inner agony as boiling within him without any break. These dark days of affliction ambushed him suddenly, catching him off guard when he was expecting peace. The continuous churning inside leaves him with neither physical ease nor mental rest.

Job's skin has turned dark and sickly, not from outdoor sun exposure, but from the burning heat of his disease and grief. When he appears in public, his pain is so overwhelming that he cannot contain himself and breaks down crying aloud for help.

Job feels like a brother to wild jackals and ostriches that dwell alone in desolate ruins. His screams and groans of anguish sound just like the shrill, eerie wails those desert animals make in the night.
Job describes the terrible physical symptoms of his sickness. His inflamed skin has blackened, cracked, and peeled away from his body, while an unrelenting fever burns like fire inside his bones.

Instruments of celebration like the harp and flute, which Job once enjoyed in happier times, now produce only funeral notes. All joy has departed from his household, and his life has been completely given over to the sounds of weeping and grief.
